meta: Heidenreich J, Pfister D, Steenbock O, Rieger C, Heidenreich A. In welchem Ausmaß sind Salvage-Operationen bei Tumoren des Urogenitaltrakts sinnvoll? Die Urologie 2026;65:145–154. DOI 10.1007/s00120-025-02748-6

EAU Guidelines on Testicular Cancer 2026, chapter 6 (6.3.2.2 and 6.3.3.1), full text checked on 21.09.2026. Full-text comparison with the relevant EAU guidelines for prostate, urothelial and renal cell carcinoma is still pending; correct answers to those questions rely on the source article.
10 questions across 6 topic areas, approximately 30 minutes

Three questions carry ⚠. Much of the article summarises case series from the same research group. PEACE-V-STORM is cited as evidence for salvage surgery although the reported figures favour pelvic radiotherapy; the questions follow the figures. Internally contradictory figures were not used, such as a lower probability of biochemical recurrence at ten years than at five.
sources: Primary source: Heidenreich J, Pfister D, Steenbock O, Rieger C, Heidenreich A (2026) In welchem Ausmaß sind Salvage-Operationen bei Tumoren des Urogenitaltrakts sinnvoll? Urologie 65:145–154. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00120-025-02748-6
Guideline: EAU Guidelines on Testicular Cancer 2026, chapter 6 Disease Management, sections 6.3.2.2 and 6.3.3.1. Full text online, accessed 21.09.2026.
Study: Ost P et al. (2025) PEACE V-STORM, randomised phase II study comparing metastasis-directed treatment with elective nodal irradiation. Lancet Oncol 26:695–706 (cited from the primary source).

Study: Bravi CA et al. (2020) Long-term outcomes of salvage lymph node dissection. Eur Urol 78:661–669; Knipper S et al. (2023) PSMA-radioguided salvage lymph node dissection. Eur Urol 83:62–69; Fossati N et al. (2019) Eur Urol 75:176–183 (cited from the primary source).

Study: Chade DC et al. (2011) Eur Urol 60:205–210 and Heidenreich A et al. (2010) Eur Urol 57:437–443 on salvage prostatectomy; Grubmüller B et al. (2021) Curr Oncol 28:2881–2892, systematic review (cited from the primary source).

Study: Culp SH et al. (2014) Local treatment in metastatic prostate cancer, SEER analysis. Eur Urol 65:1058–1066; Heidenreich A et al. (2018) Cytoreductive prostatectomy with skeletal metastases. Eur Urol Oncol 1:46–53 (cited from the primary source).

Study: Ji J et al. (2025) Metastasectomy in bladder cancer, systematic review and meta-analysis. Int J Urol 32:1552–1560; Dursun F et al. (2022) Urol Oncol 40:61.e21–e28, National Cancer Database analysis (cited from the primary source).

Study: Blanco-Fernández G et al. (2022) PANMEKID, resection of pancreatic metastases from renal cell carcinoma. Eur J Surg Oncol 48:133–141; Macherey S et al. (2017) Lung metastasis surgery, meta-analysis. Urologe 56:1025–1030 (cited from the primary source).

Study: Capitanio U et al. (2009) Perioperative mortality after retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, population-based. Urology 74:373–377; Fléchon A et al. (2010) BJU Int 106:779–785 (cited from the primary source).

axes.C: Local treatment in metastatic prostate cancer
axes.E: Metastasis surgery in renal cell carcinoma

A: Candidate for salvage prostatectomy: organ-confined recurrence, imaging-negative nodes, long PSA doubling time [Q].
mpMRI and PSMA-PET/CT are essential before deciding [Q].
5-year biochemical recurrence-free survival: 71.4% for organ-confined disease, 50% with seminal vesicle invasion, 30% with nodal involvement [Q].
B: PEACE V-STORM: 4-year metastasis-free survival 63% after metastasis-directed therapy versus 76% after pelvic radiotherapy [Q].
The realistic aim of salvage lymph node dissection is to defer hormone therapy, not cure [Q].
Postoperative PSA above 0.3 ng/ml: more recurrences and higher cancer-specific mortality; early androgen deprivation improves survival [Q].
C: Cytoreductive prostatectomy: retrospective data only; response to induction treatment is the selection criterion [Q].
Palliative pelvic surgery requires ECOG 0 to 1, normal CRP and albumin, and resectability on MRI [Q].
After palliative pelvic surgery, symptom-free survival is 89% at one year and 66% at three years [Q].
D: No clear criteria in urothelial carcinoma: meta-analyses conflict and the database analysis shows no advantage [Q].
Isolated lung or nodal metastases with complete resectability are most likely to benefit [Q].
Favourable markers: fewer than five involved nodes, CRP below 1.0 mg/dl, solitary visceral metastasis [Q].
E: Curative metastasectomy means R0 for all lesions: median survival 40.75 versus 14.8 months after incomplete resection [Q].
Pancreatic metastases grow indolently; 5-year survival after resection 83%, but morbidity 60.9% [Q].
Brain metastases: focal treatment plus systemic therapy; whole-brain irradiation is inferior [Q].
F: Residual tumour resection outside specialist centres: higher 30-day mortality, more incomplete resections and recurrences [Q].
At specialist centres, perioperative mortality falls from 6% to 0.8% [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.3.1].
Guideline discordance of almost 40% is the real care problem, not surgical feasibility [Q].

questions.objective: Can identify a suitable candidate for salvage prostatectomy after radiotherapy.
questions.reference: Article: radical salvage prostatectomy after radiotherapy
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man has a biopsy-proven local recurrence six years after external beam radiotherapy, Gleason 3+4. PSA is 3.2 ng/ml with a doubling time of 14 months. Multiparametric MRI shows an organ-confined lesion, PSMA-PET/CT no nodal or distant metastases. He is continent, ECOG 0. Treatment is to be defined.

opts.A: Lifelong androgen deprivation without local therapy
opts.B: Salvage prostatectomy at an experienced centre
opts.C: Salvage prostatectomy at once, without further imaging
opts.E: Docetaxel chemotherapy because of the recurrence

rat.A: Misconception: recurrence after radiotherapy is no longer curable. More than 90% of patients nevertheless receive non-curative androgen deprivation [Q].
rat.B: Organ-confined recurrence, negative nodes and a long doubling time are exactly the constellation in which salvage prostatectomy works [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: imaging can be skipped. Multiparametric MRI and PSMA-PET/CT are indispensable before the decision [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: waiting costs nothing. Once distant metastases appear, the curative option is gone [X].
rat.E: Misconception: systemic therapy as the next escalation. For a locally confined recurrence it is not the first choice [Q].

questions.core: The profile fits: locally confined recurrence, imaging-negative nodes, long PSA doubling time and a long interval since radiotherapy [Q].
questions.ev: In large single-centre series, metastasis-free survival at ten years is 75 to 80% and cancer-specific survival 80 to 90% [Q]. Complication rates are given as 2 to 5%, rectal injury below 1.5% [Q]. Biochemical recurrence-free survival at five years is 71.4% for organ-confined recurrence [Q].
questions.prax: Incontinence is the central counselling issue: 20 to 40% depending on the preceding radiotherapy, with recovery taking eight months on average [Q]. The indication belongs in the multidisciplinary tumour board and the operation in a centre experienced in salvage surgery [Q].
questions.merk: Salvage prostatectomy: organ-confined, node-negative, long doubling time, imaging complete.
questions.flag: The results come from retrospective single-centre series with substantial patient selection; randomised comparisons with other salvage procedures are lacking.

questions.objective: Can recognise unfavourable selection features before salvage prostatectomy and infer the need for restraint.
questions.reference: Article: radical salvage prostatectomy, risk factors
questions.vignette: A 71-year-old man requests salvage prostatectomy after radiotherapy. Multiparametric MRI shows recurrence with seminal vesicle infiltration, PSMA-PET/CT a suspicious pelvic node. PSA is 6.8 ng/ml, doubling time 4 months, ECOG 1. Management is to be defined.
questions.lead: How should his request be judged?

opts.C: Offer focal salvage therapy of the recurrent lesion
opts.D: Restraint; discuss systemic therapy in the tumour board
opts.E: Repeat radiotherapy of the recurrence without further work-up

rat.A: Misconception: the patient's wish replaces selection. This very constellation argues against a curative claim [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: more surgery compensates for the starting position. Positive nodes were associated with more recurrences, more metastatic spread and higher mortality [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: focal therapy as the gentle solution. It addresses neither the seminal vesicles nor the node [X].
rat.D: Seminal vesicle infiltration, a positive node and a short doubling time mark the group with the least benefit [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: repeat radiotherapy without a concept. Imaging and the tumour board precede every salvage decision [Q].

questions.core: Resectability is not the same as a chance of cure: these risk features markedly reduce the benefit of surgery [Q].
questions.ev: With seminal vesicle invasion, biochemical recurrence-free survival at five years falls to 50%, with nodal involvement to 30%, compared with 71.4% for organ-confined recurrence [Q]. Mean biochemical progression-free survival is 31.4 months with nodal metastases versus 61.8 months without [Q]. In a series of 334 patients, positive nodes were associated with increased overall mortality [Q].
questions.prax: The indication for salvage surgery always belongs in the multidisciplinary tumour board, together with the alternative of systemic therapy [Q]. Counselling names the realistic chance of cure, not only technical feasibility [Q].
questions.merk: Seminal vesicle invasion or a positive node: salvage prostatectomy loses its curative claim.

questions.objective: Can weigh the randomised evidence against metastasis-directed surgery in nodal recurrence.
questions.reference: Article: salvage lymph node dissection, PEACE V-STORM
questions.vignette: A 64-year-old man has biochemical recurrence two years after radical prostatectomy, PSA 1.8 ng/ml. PSMA-PET/CT shows two suspicious pelvic nodes and no distant metastases. He is hormone-naive and asks for metastasis-directed therapy. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Pelvic radiotherapy with a boost plus androgen deprivation
opts.B: Salvage lymph node dissection with curative intent
opts.C: PSMA-radioguided salvage lymphadenectomy as the standard
opts.D: Androgen deprivation alone without any local measure

rat.A: In the randomised trial, metastasis-free survival at four years was 76% after pelvic radiotherapy versus 63% after metastasis-directed therapy [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: visible nodes are surgically curable. Very few patients achieve cure [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: the radioguided technique makes the procedure a standard. In the largest cohort of 364 patients only 45% reached a PSA nadir below 0.2 ng/ml [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: without surgery only hormones remain. The combination of radiotherapy and androgen deprivation was superior in the comparison [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: a low PSA permits waiting. The evidence supports early treatment of nodal recurrence [Q].

questions.core: For oligonodal recurrence a randomised trial exists, and it does not favour surgery [Q].
questions.ev: In PEACE V-STORM, 196 patients received either metastasis-directed therapy by lymphadenectomy or stereotactic radiotherapy with six months of androgen deprivation, or pelvic radiotherapy with 45 Gy plus a boost of 65 Gy to the PET-positive nodes; the primary endpoint was metastasis-free survival [Q]. Retrospective series of salvage lymphadenectomy show biochemical recurrence-free survival at two years of only 32% [Q].
questions.prax: If surgery is performed nonetheless, the realistic aim is deferral of hormone therapy [Q]. The article calls the results of this trial excellent without stating that they came out against the surgical approach [X].
questions.merk: Oligonodal recurrence: pelvic radiotherapy with a boost plus hormone therapy beats metastasis-directed surgery.
questions.flag: The article cites PEACE-V-STORM data as evidence for salvage surgery, although the reported figures favour pelvic radiotherapy.

questions.objective: Can state the realistic treatment aim of salvage lymph node dissection.
questions.reference: Article: salvage lymph node dissection, long-term outcomes
questions.vignette: A 66-year-old man is scheduled for salvage lymph node dissection for two PSMA-positive pelvic nodes after multidisciplinary discussion. He asks what the procedure realistically means for him. Consent discussion before surgery.

opts.A: Cure is to be expected in the majority of patients
opts.B: After the procedure, hormone therapy is no longer needed
opts.C: Realistically, a longer time without hormone therapy
opts.D: A PSA nadir below 0.2 is reached almost always
opts.E: The risk of recurrence in the first year is under five percent

rat.A: Misconception: visible metastases are surgically curable. Clinical recurrence-free survival at ten years is 31% [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: the operation spares hormone therapy for good. 77% of patients received it during follow-up [Q].
rat.C: The main indication lies in extending the systemic therapy-free interval, which with good selection can reach 42 months [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: the nadir is the rule. In the largest series 45% reached it within three months [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: early recurrence is rare. One in four patients recurs within the first year [Q].

questions.core: The procedure postpones the start of androgen deprivation; as a rule it does not cure [Q].
questions.ev: In a cohort of 189 patients, clinical and biochemical recurrence-free survival at ten years were 31% and 11%; 145 patients received androgen deprivation at a median of 41 months [Q]. Early recurrence within the first year was associated with cancer-specific mortality at three years of 20% versus 1.4% [Q]. Predictors are Gleason grade 5, the PSA level and three or more positive spots on PET/CT [Q].
questions.prax: A postoperative PSA above 0.3 ng/ml is associated with more recurrences and higher cancer-specific mortality; early androgen deprivation then improves survival [Q]. Counselling should name the aim before the patient expects cure [X].
questions.merk: Salvage lymphadenectomy: deferral of hormone therapy as the aim, cure is the exception.

questions.objective: Can classify cytoreductive prostatectomy as a case-by-case decision and a study question.
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with de novo metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer and three bone lesions has a PSA fall to 0.1 ng/ml after six months of systemic therapy. He has read about cytoreductive prostatectomy and asks for it. Management is to be defined.
questions.lead: How should his request be judged?

opts.A: Offer cytoreductive prostatectomy as standard therapy
opts.B: Decline surgery, no benefit has been shown anywhere
opts.C: Perform surgery irrespective of treatment response
opts.D: Consider surgery only for local symptoms
opts.E: Individual decision in the tumour board or in a trial

rat.A: Misconception: favourable registry data make a standard. Prospective randomised evidence is lacking [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: no randomisation, no signal. Several series show consistent advantages in highly selected patients [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: response is a side issue. It is the decisive selection criterion [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: only palliation counts. Local symptom control is an additional argument, not the only one [Q].
rat.E: The article itself calls the operation a highly individual treatment decision resting on retrospective data [Q].

questions.core: The patient meets the published selection criteria, but the evidence remains retrospective: decide in the tumour board, preferably within a trial [Q].
questions.ev: In the SEER analysis, overall and cancer-specific survival at five years were 67.4% and 75.8% versus 22.5% and 48.7% under androgen deprivation alone [Q]. In the largest series of 113 selected patients, median overall survival was 85.4 months [Q]. As prerequisites the article names a PSA nadir below 0.2 ng/ml or a fall of more than 80% after induction therapy, plus a low metastatic burden [Q].
questions.prax: One advantage lies in avoiding later obstruction: in the case-control study 71% of patients treated with hormones alone needed a palliative intervention, none in the surgical group [Q]. The lack of randomised evidence belongs in the consent discussion [X].
questions.merk: Cytoreductive prostatectomy: only after good response, with low burden, in the tumour board and preferably in trials.
questions.flag: The recommendation relies predominantly on retrospective series from the same research group. Guidelines are cautious about surgery for metastatic prostate cancer outside studies; local radiotherapy for low metastatic burden is included there.

questions.objective: Can indicate palliative pelvic surgery for symptomatic locally advanced prostate cancer.
questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man with castration-resistant, locally advanced prostate cancer has recurrent bladder tamponade, an indwelling catheter and bilateral nephrostomies. ECOG 1, CRP and albumin within range, pelvic MRI shows a resectable finding. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Palliative radical pelvic surgery at a centre
opts.B: Continuing the catheter and repeated clot evacuations
opts.C: Palliative systemic therapy only, without local measures
opts.D: Pelvic surgery irrespective of performance status
opts.E: Urinary diversion alone without tumour resection

rat.A: With a resectable finding, ECOG 1 and normal inflammatory and nutritional parameters, the procedure can control symptoms durably [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: repeated interventions are the gentler route. They consume transfusions and hospital days without solving anything [X].
rat.C: Misconception: systemic therapy solves the local problem. With castration resistance and obstruction it usually does not [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: performance status is secondary. Raised CRP and low albumin argue against the procedure [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: diversion suffices. The bleeding source and rectal compression remain [X].

questions.core: Palliative tumour surgery in the pelvis is not overtreatment here but the most effective symptom control [Q].
questions.ev: In the authors' experience, 80% of patients need radical cystoprostatectomy with an ileal conduit, and 10% each a prostatectomy with bladder neck closure or an exenteration [Q]. Symptom-free survival at one and three years was 89% and 66%, overall survival 89% and 42.4% [Q]. Morbidity corresponded to that of classical radical cystectomy [Q].
questions.prax: Resectability is clarified on pelvic MRI before the extent is decided [Q]. The procedure belongs in a centre experienced in pelvic surgery and urinary diversion [Q].
questions.merk: Symptomatic pelvic recurrence with good performance status: palliative radical surgery instead of a permanent catheter.

questions.objective: Can use the contradictory evidence for metastasis surgery in urothelial carcinoma to make an individual decision.
questions.reference: Article: metastasis surgery in bladder urothelial carcinoma
questions.vignette: A 61-year-old man has a stable solitary lung metastasis after four cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy for metastatic urothelial carcinoma, with no other evidence of tumour. ECOG 0, no relevant comorbidity. A colleague proposes metastasectomy. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Metastasectomy as standard practice after response
opts.B: Decline metastasectomy, the benefit has been refuted
opts.C: In the tumour board as a single case with complete resection
opts.D: Offer resection even with several metastatic sites
opts.E: Repeat chemotherapy instead of any local measure

rat.A: Misconception: response justifies surgery in general. Clear criteria cannot be derived from the data [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: one negative database analysis refutes the benefit. Other analyses show clear advantages [Q].
rat.C: Those most likely to benefit have an isolated lung or nodal metastasis and complete resectability [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: more resection is better. Extrapulmonary disease markedly worsens the outcome [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: systemic therapy replaces the local decision. With a stable solitary metastasis surgery is worth discussing [Q].

questions.core: The evidence supports no rule, only a selection: isolated metastasis, complete resectability, stable disease on systemic therapy [Q].
questions.ev: A meta-analysis of eight publications with 15,139 patients found a survival benefit of metastasectomy, whereas an analysis of the National Cancer Database after propensity score matching found none [Q]. In an analysis of 19 retrospective studies with 616 patients, median overall survival was most favourable for lung metastases at 46.2 months, 31.2 months for nodal and 29 months for other sites [Q]. Fewer than five involved nodes and a CRP below 1.0 mg/dl are favourable [Q].
questions.prax: The decision belongs in the tumour board, not in the clinic alone [Q]. If extrapulmonary tumour remains, the rationale for surgery falls away [Q].
questions.merk: Urothelial carcinoma: metastasectomy only for an isolated, completely resectable metastasis with stable disease.
questions.flag: Two meta-analyses reach opposite conclusions; prospective data are lacking, and selection explains part of the reported benefit.

questions.objective: Can apply the principle of complete metastasis resection in renal cell carcinoma.
questions.reference: Article: complete metastasis resection is always required
questions.vignette: A 63-year-old man has three resectable lung metastases of clear cell renal cell carcinoma three years after nephrectomy, plus a non-resectable metastasis in the iliac bone. ECOG 0, no symptoms. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Resect all lung metastases and leave the bone lesion
opts.B: Thoracoscopic resection before any systemic therapy
opts.C: Resect bone metastasis and lung lesions together
opts.D: Systemic therapy plus focal treatment of the bone lesion
opts.E: Observation until symptoms or progression occur

rat.A: Misconception: partial resection brings partial benefit. The survival advantage depends on complete resection [Q].
rat.B: Misconception: surgery first, regardless of the overall picture. With non-resectable residual disease the curative perspective is missing [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: everything must be operated. The bone lesion is not resectable but can be treated stereotactically [Q].
rat.D: Without the possibility of an R0 situation for all lesions, systemic therapy takes precedence, supplemented by focal measures [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: waiting is neutral. The disease is metastatic and requires treatment [X].

questions.core: Metastasectomy with curative intent presupposes that all lesions can be removed completely; that is not the case here [Q].
questions.ev: An analysis of eight studies showed median overall survival of 40.75 months after complete resection versus 14.8 months after incomplete resection [Q]. R0 resection is considered the prognostic factor of greatest relevance [Q]. Skeletal oligometastases are, in the article's view, better treated with stereotactic radiotherapy [Q]. Lung metastases are the most common site at 70% [Q].
questions.prax: If only one resectable site remains after systemic therapy, metastasectomy can be reconsidered [X]. Isolated lung metastases can be removed thoracoscopically with low morbidity [Q]. A long disease-free interval between nephrectomy and metastasis predicts a more favourable outcome [Q].
questions.merk: Renal cell carcinoma: metastasectomy only if all lesions can be removed R0.

questions.objective: Can indicate resection of a pancreatic metastasis from renal cell carcinoma and state its morbidity.
questions.vignette: A 70-year-old man presents nine years after nephrectomy with a solitary 3 cm metastasis in the pancreatic tail. No other lesions on imaging, ECOG 0, fit for surgery. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Systemic therapy alone because of the pancreatic site
opts.B: Offer resection and counsel about the morbidity
opts.C: Biopsy and follow-up imaging in six months
opts.D: Stereotactic radiotherapy instead of any resection
opts.E: Total pancreatectomy because of multifocality risk

rat.A: Misconception: the site forbids surgery. Long-term results are particularly favourable here [Q].
rat.B: A solitary pancreatic metastasis after a long interval argues for resection, albeit with a high complication rate [Q].
rat.C: Misconception: indolent growth permits waiting. The advantage lies in complete resection [Q].
rat.D: Misconception: radiotherapy as an equivalent substitute. The data presented support resection [Q].
rat.E: Misconception: maximum radicality. Distal pancreatectomy is the most common technique, used in half of cases [Q].

questions.core: Pancreatic metastases of renal cell carcinoma grow indolently; with a solitary lesion and a long interval, resection is well justified [Q].
questions.ev: In the PANMEDIC study of 116 resected patients, overall survival at one, three and five years was 96%, 88% and 83%, and disease-free survival 73%, 49% and 35% [Q]. The mean time between nephrectomy and pancreatic metastasis was 87 months [Q]. An interval under ten years and previous extrapancreatic metastases are unfavourable [Q].
questions.prax: Morbidity is substantial: 60.9% postoperative complications, of which 14% are Clavien-Dindo IIIa or higher [Q]. The decision is taken together with visceral surgery [X].
questions.merk: Solitary pancreatic metastasis after a long interval: resect, but counsel about a complication rate above 60%.

questions.objective: Can recognise a residual mass judged inoperable elsewhere as a reason to seek a second opinion at a specialist centre.
questions.reference: Article: salvage operations in testicular germ cell tumours; EAU Testicular Cancer 2026, 6.3.3.1
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old man with metastatic non-seminoma has a complex retroperitoneal residual mass with vascular contact after chemotherapy. Elsewhere he was deemed inoperable and is to receive further chemotherapy. Markers have normalised, ECOG 0. Management is to be defined.

opts.A: Two further cycles of chemotherapy as proposed
opts.B: Radiotherapy of the residual mass as an alternative to surgery
opts.C: Observation as long as markers remain normal
opts.D: Biopsy of the residual mass to guide treatment
opts.E: Second opinion and resection at a centre

rat.A: Misconception: more chemotherapy solves the surgical problem. Residual masses with teratoma do not respond [X].
rat.B: Misconception: radiotherapy replaces resection in non-seminoma. There is no basis for this [X].
rat.C: Misconception: normal markers permit waiting. Residual masses above 1 cm are resected [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.2.2].
rat.D: Misconception: the biopsy decides. It is not representative and does not change the indication for resection [X].
rat.E: Even potentially inoperable scenarios can be managed curatively with low morbidity at specialised centres [Q].

questions.core: In germ cell tumours, inoperability is often a question of the centre rather than of the finding [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.3.1].
questions.ev: Residual tumour resection is an integral part of curative treatment, and unlike in renal cell carcinoma all metastases are resected regardless of site [Q]. The article notes that 30-day mortality rises significantly outside specialised centres, where incomplete resections and recurrences are also more frequent [Q]. The guideline quantifies the difference: at specialised centres perioperative mortality falls from 6% to 0.8% and local recurrence from 16% to 3% [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.3.1].
questions.prax: The article names a guideline discordance of nearly 40% as the real problem of care [Q]. The limit lies in missing centralisation, not in what is surgically feasible [Q]. A second opinion costs days; a missing resection costs the chance of cure [X].
questions.merk: Complex residual mass declared inoperable elsewhere: second opinion at a centre before any further chemotherapy.

hcg.label: Prostate: local recurrence after radiotherapy
hcg.mech: Cure: 10-year metastasis-free survival 75 to 80%, cancer-specific survival 80 to 90% [Q].
hcg.step: Organ-confined recurrence, imaging-negative nodes, long PSA doubling time; mpMRI and PSMA-PET/CT before deciding [Q].
hcg.data: Single-centre series, no randomisation; incontinence 20 to 40%, with recovery over eight months [Q].

hcg.label: Prostate: nodal recurrence after prostatectomy
hcg.mech: Deferral of androgen deprivation, up to 42 months with good selection; cure is rare [Q].
hcg.step: Few PET-positive lesions, low PSA, favourable Gleason grade; pelvic radiotherapy with a boost is an alternative [Q].
hcg.data: Biochemical recurrence-free survival 32% at two years, 11% at ten years; in the randomised study 4-year metastasis-free survival was 63% versus 76% with radiotherapy [Q].

hcg.label: Prostate: cytoreductive prostatectomy
hcg.mech: Prolonging the progression-free interval and preventing local complications; no randomised survival evidence [Q].
hcg.step: Good response to induction treatment with PSA nadir below 0.2 ng/ml or decrease above 80%, low metastatic burden, tumour board [Q].
hcg.data: Registry data and case-control studies; 71% treated with hormones alone required a palliative intervention, none in the surgery group [Q].

hcg.label: Prostate: palliative pelvic surgery
hcg.mech: Symptom control for bleeding, obstruction and rectal compression [Q].
hcg.step: ECOG 0 to 1, normal CRP and albumin, resectability on pelvic MRI [Q].
hcg.data: Symptom-free survival at one and three years 89% and 66%, overall survival 89% and 42.4% [Q].

hcg.label: Urothelial carcinoma: metastasis surgery
hcg.mech: Prolonging survival in selected cases; no claim of cure across the wider population [Q].
hcg.step: Isolated lung or nodal metastasis, complete resectability, stable disease after systemic treatment [Q].
hcg.data: Contradictory: a meta-analysis of 15,139 patients shows a benefit, the database analysis after propensity score matching does not [Q].

hcg.label: Renal cell carcinoma: metastasectomy
hcg.mech: Cure only with complete resection of all lesions [Q].
hcg.step: Good general condition, R0 achievable at every site, long disease-free interval [Q].
hcg.data: Median survival 40.75 months after complete versus 14.8 months after incomplete resection; pancreatic metastases with 5-year survival of 83% [Q].

hcg.label: Germ cell tumour: residual tumour resection
hcg.mech: Curative, integral to multimodal treatment, regardless of site [Q].
hcg.step: Normalised markers, resection of all residual masses, procedure at a recognised specialist centre [Q] [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.2.2].
hcg.data: At specialist centres, perioperative mortality falls from 6% to 0.8% and local recurrence from 16% to 3% [LL EAU 2026, 6.3.3.1].

criteria: Indication discussed in an interdisciplinary tumour board
All lesions resectable with clear margins or a clear palliative aim
ECOG 0 to 1 and comorbidity permits surgery
Realistic treatment aim discussed with the patient
Procedure at a centre with the appropriate experience

transfer.title: Tumour board first
transfer.note: The article makes interdisciplinary discussion a prerequisite for every salvage indication and clarifies that resectability does not mean a higher chance of cure [Q].

robotic.title: Salvage surgery is reasonable
robotic.note: All conditions met: tumour board discussion, curative or clearly defined palliative aim, suitable general condition, informed patient and experienced surgeon [Q]. In complex scenarios, centre experience determines complication rates and completeness of resection [Q].

open.title: Assess alternatives
open.note: If a condition is missing, systemic treatment, stereotactic radiotherapy or observation are the more realistic options [Q]. In nodal prostate cancer recurrence, pelvic radiotherapy was superior to metastasis-directed surgery in the randomised comparison [Q], and skeletal oligometastases are better treated with stereotactic irradiation [Q].
